title: The Gothic & Politics: Quick Takes
abstract: Artistic works are inevitably political, often doing their most powerful ideological work when they appear distant from political concerns. The Gothic, as a genre expressive of cultural anxieties, has often responded to political concerns, while Gothic images and tropes have often found their way into political discourse. Using this as a premise, we invited a number of established scholars on the Gothic for their thoughts on the interrelationships between the Gothic and politics. As you will see, their approaches to the question range widely.Sixties activism taught us that the personal is political and that social relationships are always premised upon power flows and the subjugation of large communities. But what happens when the political becomes personal, openly exclusionary in its dislike of what it perceives as liberal humanist values? When the antigender agenda gradually takes over Europe through far-right discourse and populist governments and when DEI programs are rolled back in the United States, including the elimination of areas of study directly connected to identity politics now recast as “wasteful”?One answer is civic: The “No Kings” (also known as “No Dictators” or “No Tyrants”) demonstrations—rallying cries of denial and resistance that demand actual change in the real world and challenge unilateral governmental decisions. Another is cultural: The Gothic becomes less a source of anxiety and much more one of possibility and expansion, a tool to help us (re)think the world according to different parameters.As discrimination, fear, and oppression become the dominant language, the liberatory messages in the Gothic shift from subtext to text. Get Out (Peele, 2017) offers an early example of how directors who have traditionally existed outside of the entertainment industries that diagnose our nightmares are particularly keen to formulate the argument that “the bad guy is society,” as Jordan Peele puts it. And perhaps this is partly why monsters have become sources of sympathy and comfort too; we empathize a lot more with the experience of exclusion, and we are much more likely than ever to question everything, especially authority. The Gothic’s development of a politics of transformation and its desire to embrace otherness can therefore be seen as balm for the soul as well as another expression of revolutionary feelings in times of crisis.Whether conceived of as a genre, a mode, a style, or simply a discursive practice of reading texts within a particular critical framework, the Gothic has always been political. Its ghosts are routinely deployed to redress cultural traumas, while its monsters appear as stand-ins for tyrannical regimes and embodiments of difference. Concerned with boundaries that it simultaneously transgresses and reinscribes, the Gothic recognizes that liminality unsettles power relations and can pose a threat to the dominant order. At the same time, it alerts us that power is always in flux, that the line separating heroes from villains is often blurry, and that new monsters are ever ready to be born.Gothic narratives have long been used to address social injustices and political fears. They comment on political and cultural practices that frequently depend on othering women, foreigners, immigrants, political dissidents, or members of the lower classes, exposing divisions and imbalances of power. Gothic tropes have been mobilized to reinforce and to subvert identities—weaponized to demonize groups that challenge the dominant social order, but also to critique the marginalization of such groups. This duality is inherent in its design, as Gothic narrative dynamics arise from the tension between desire or sympathy for the Other and the fear of being consumed. It is also a reminder that monstrosity is invariably a construction, used as a signifier of difference for political ends.When Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) tried to convey the totalizing power of the State to his readers, he personified it into a creature—a leviathan, a giant monster with superhuman strength and opaque purposes. That’s how his audience understood agency. But in the twentieth century, we became accustomed to thinking of decentralized forms of power—stored within anonymous bureaucracies—effectively reversing Hobbes’s notion of agency.We began thinking of persons as systems—routinized causal structures with conditioned inputs and behavioral outputs. From B. F. Skinner to Michel Foucault to the latest AI algorithmically guided purchase you made online, we have been disassembled into distributed machines, governed by a calculus of hedonistic forces and made efficient by consumer capitalism. We frequently think of ourselves as cogs in a machine. Consequently, the way we think about cruelty changes, and we tilt away from demons, sinners, and even psychopaths, toward economic systems, complex institutions, and dehumanizing corporations.My son’s mother is Chinese, and she was born in mainland China during the Cultural Revolution. Her father was considered dangerous simply for being a professor and was sent to a reeducation camp. During this time, many Western novels and films were banned on the mainland, but she was allowed, even encouraged, to read Charles Dickens novels. All over the communist world, Dickens’s stories, with their impoverished characters, child labor sweatshops, and squalid industrial backgrounds, were embraced as “evidence” of the alienating and dehumanizing effects of capitalism. Indeed, this is how I was encouraged to read Dickens in college—a parade of cruel oppressions, an indictment of the capitalist system.Closer reading of Dickens, however, reveals nothing of the sort. Yes, life is hard according to Dickens, but the cause of misery in most of his novels is the cruel antagonist who lacks good character. Think of Miss Havisham, Fagin, Bill Sikes, Madame Defarge, or Ebenezer Scrooge. The solution to suffering in Dickens’s stories is greater individual kindness. Misery happens in factories and impoverished underworlds, yes, but most real causes of suffering are selfish, greedy, or cold-hearted individuals. Most Gothic fiction is conservative in this way. Orwell found this funny and maddening, and his own 1984 can be read as a counterpunch to Dickens’s “naïve theory” of mean-spirited individuals. Cruelty for Orwell was systemic.In contemporary U.S. politics, the left agrees with Orwell and the right agrees with Dickens. Yet in truth, the two writers are less opponents than complements. Dickens captures the drama of the heart, where cruelty and compassion shape the fate of individuals; Orwell captures the machinery of history, where systems grind down lives regardless of virtue. To read them together is to see human suffering in stereo—one channel intimate, the other monumental—and to be reminded that the full story of our condition requires both.Conspiracies do exist, but exaggerated and overblown conspiracy theories have little basis in reality, needing only a minimum effort in “doing your own research” to uncover the facts. The increasingly common claim that the World Economic Forum is a sinister cabal with secret plans to track or even depopulate societies through vaccines, abolish private property, and restrict movement to fifteen-minute zones can be assessed simply by reading the articles published on the organization’s own website. Whatever their nefarious plans are, they seem to have missed the memo about keeping them secret.To anyone familiar with the Gothic, these are well-worn tropes that have been recycled throughout history and in fiction. The suggestion that the consumption of insects might prove to be one way of providing a source of sustainable protein is a much less compelling story than a fiction of being force fed them like an episode of Survivor written by Matthew “Monk” Lewis. In this way too, the “Great Reset” (a relatively dull plan for post-COVID economic recovery) can become a viral narrative when combined with a version of the centuries-old anti-Semitic blood libel.In a world of global challenges that are all too real, the study of the Gothic can be a powerful tool for combating misinformation and encouraging critical thinking when faced with such narratives, emerging like Gothic fiction itself as a response to times of extreme communal anxiety and uncertainty.A little-cited context for the development of the “Female Gothic” around the turn of the nineteenth century is the situation that Marx and Engels described as the dissolution of the working-class family. This crisis erupted out of the extremely laissez-faire labor market in early industrializing Britain, which employed men, women, and children at long hours and for little pay, leaving next to no time, money, and energy available for activities of social reproduction that are vital to maintaining a workforce: having and raising children, housework, cooking, sleep.
